#354. Google rolls out Gemini 4 Hydrogen, finally replacing 3.8 Flash

Gemini 4 Hydrogen isn’t getting a slow, security-conscious release like Carbon and Argon.

Google is continuing its elemental AI naming scheme with the new Gemini 4 Hydrogen. These names are less descriptive than the Pro/Flash monikers of earlier releases, but Hydrogen’s purpose is clear: It replaces the faster, more economical Flash models most people in Google’s ecosystem use.

With Google’s recent Argon and Carbon releases, the rollout was staged and began with cybersecurity researchers. Even when general availability began, Google restricted access to users paying for its most expensive AI subscription. The limits for Hydrogen are much more relaxed, with access beginning immediately. This model has replaced Gemini 3.8 Flash across the company’s products.

Google claims that Hydrogen represents a major improvement versus the previous Flash model. It runs in one of four thinking levels (low, medium, high, and the new xhigh), and even in high mode, it’s 2.5 times faster than Flash 3.8. Plus, it reduces “fabricated claims” by more than 5x, according to Google’s analysis. Users will also see gains in code generation, with Hydrogen more than tripling 3.8 Flash’s score in Terminal-Bench. In some cases, Hydrogen even trades blows with Argon. It managed a score of 54 in the popular Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index with xhigh mode versus 50 for Argon.

Google believes Hydrogen will be a key part of how developers work with agentic coding tools. While it still positions Argon and Carbon as the best for long-horizon tasks and security, Hydrogen’s speed makes it ideal for generating simpler code and running tests without blowing through token budgets.

Hydrogen is also being integrated with Google Search, which the company says is the biggest update to its AI-powered search tools ever. The new model should better handle long, multipart questions, and the responses in both AI Overviews and AI Mode will have more visual elements. The company also claims Hydrogen’s fan-out search has been tuned to link to more sources, but we’ve heard that from Google before.

#351. The Elder Scrolls' most obscure adventure gets a 4K PC makeover

N-Gage exclusive Shadowkey gets an AI-coded glow-up with plenty of new features.

So, you think you’re an Elder Scrolls superfan? You say you’ve been there since The Elder Scrolls Arena on MS-DOS and have logged hundreds of hours in The Elder Scrolls Online? You say you’ve bought all of the roughly 5,000 re-releases and remasters of Skyrim that have been made available in the last 15 years?

Tell me, then: What do you think of The Elder Scrolls Travels: Shadowkey?

What’s that? You’ve never played Shadowkey? You weren’t there day one back in 2004, Nokia N-Gage in hand, ready to experience the game’s 176 x 208 resolution mobile hack-and-slash RPG combat for yourself? And you call yourself a real Elder Scrolls fan?

Well, don’t worry. Now you can fill in this crucial gap in your history without even having to track down functional, decades-old N-Gage hardware. That’s thanks to Shadowkey: Reforged, a free fan-made PC port that pairs updated art with the original game files and scripts for an upscaled, 4K experience that runs natively on PC, no N-Gage or emulator needed.

Moving from a pre-iPhone mobile game to a modern PC obviously comes with major graphical upgrades, powered by a completely rewritten PC graphics engine. What was once a cramped portrait orientation on the N-Gage has now been expanded for a 16:9 monitor standard that displays at up to 120 fps (though the game’s logic still matches the original game’s 25 fps). In addition to newly retextured character and environmental models, the new port also sports small touches like bloom lighting, rippling water, and an upgraded interface with sharper text rendering than was possible on an ancient mobile phone.

Using the original game files (which you can obtain from an easy-to-find legitimate copy of the game, of course) means that Reforged‘s quests, dialogue, and game rules are “worked out from the original program,” as the game’s website puts it. That said, the game’s “Modern” mode adds a few touches like smarter enemy AI, fall damage, searchable containers, and a fast travel system that are missing from the original game (and from Reforged‘s more authentic “Classic” mode). The Modern mode also includes some welcome quality-of-life improvements like controller rumble, a smoother on-screen interface, and “better death poses.”

Those with a disposition against vibe-coded clones and ports should know that Reforged author Dan Whelan writes that he used “AI to assist with coding and building the engine, and with debugging,” as well as for the creation of “most of the modern, higher resolution artwork.” But those who are OK with this AI assistance should be happy to see the project moved from its first playable version in late October to a full-featured “release day” build for Windows, Mac, and Android that came out Wednesday. Whelan has been releasing daily updates to the project and seems set to continue, if the current “Version 0.2.9” designation is any indication.

The inherent limitations of 2000s-era N-Gage game development (which helped earn the original release some middling review scores) are still pretty apparent in even this Reforged remake. Still, it’s nice that Elder Scrolls completionists can now experience one of the series’ least-played releases. At the very least, it’s something to tinker with as we all continue the long wait for Elder Scrolls VI.

#348. Is 1TB enough storage for your Xbox Series X? Here's what gamers should know

Size really is everything when you're considering what storage to go for for your next games console purchase.

The Xbox Series X may not be the hottest console anymore, but if you can find it for a more reasonable price than Microsoft is currently charging, it still has plenty going for it. There's backwards compatibility going back decades, and partly because of that, Xbox Game Pass remains a better deal than any subscription Sony is offering. I personally prefer the Xbox gamepad design, as subjective as that point might be.

Most Series X models also start with a relatively generous 1TB of storage, whereas the PlayStation 5 Slim comes with 825GB, and Nintendo's Switch 2 has just 256GB. That matters, since even if you opt for disc-based games, installing hundreds of gigabytes of data is pretty much de facto in 2026. It's impossible for any optical drive to match the speeds of an SSD.

Is 1TB going to be enough for you? Most likely the answer is yes. But if you're a truly hardcore gamer, it can be worth spending more upfront on a 2TB model. Trying to cope with limited storage later is going to be a hassle, and an expensive one at that.

On any console, a base amount of storage is automatically consumed by the operating system. It's unavoidable. In the case of the Series X, you may be left with 802GB (or less) of usable space for all the games and other apps you want to install.

For some of you, this may be more than you'll ever need. Increasingly, however, the biggest games are surpassing the 100GB mark. Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 consumes about 137GB for its single-player campaign   — never mind the multiplayer most players come to the series for — while Grand Theft Auto 6 devours a whopping 225GB. Depending on what you choose to play, a 1TB Xbox might only have enough room for a handful of games at a time, forcing you to delete anything that isn't in active rotation.

These footprints might sound absurd if you're new to high-end gaming systems, or you've been out of the loop for a while, but it all boils down to media assets. A game with native 4K support naturally demands high-resolution textures to match. On top of that, games frequently include many gigabytes of map, model and audio data. We're a long way from the Xbox 360 days, when resolution normally topped out at 720p, and simply being able to render a vast landscape in Red Dead Redemption was a big deal.

Although you can expand your Xbox's storage after-the-fact, there are some tough limits at play. Most significantly, if you want a drive you can actually run your games from, you're going to need an Xbox-compatible NVMe expansion card. Most external SSDs (like the one above) can only store Series X/S games, not load them, which seems pointless unless you hate the idea of redownloading your games just that much.

That wouldn't be such an issue if the expansion cards weren't so pricey. From Microsoft, a 1TB Seagate card is at least $200, and you'll spend far more than that if you want 2 or 4TB. Conversely, it a 2TB Galaxy Black Xbox is just $50 more than the 1TB Robot White version . Both are arguably overpriced when bought new, but there's only so much anyone can do about that with AI-inflated memory prices.

Let's reiterate something here — 1TB may well be a livable amount for some gamers. Many 2D and indie games fall under the 100GB mark, and some of us (including yours truly) rarely play more than one or two games at a time. If most of your free time is spent playing console games, however, that Galaxy Black Xbox should be your target, whether new or used.

#347. Samsung may be getting rid of another One UI feature

Samsung's news aggregator may not be long for this world.

If you've ever stumbled upon a feed of news headlines while swiping through your Galaxy phone's home screen, you've probably used Samsung News, even if you've never opened the app itself. However, this page may not be around much longer, as Galaxy owners in certain regions have received a notice that Samsung will be discontinuing Samsung News later this year. For now, only users in South Korea and India have been told that News is going away, but outlets like SamMobile claim it is "highly likely" that the service will be discontinued in other markets as well.

Along with the app, Samsung News widgets and the media page on the home screen in these regions will also stop working on December 21, 2026. Engadget reached out to Samsung to ask whether American Galaxy users should expect the same change, but we haven't heard back as of this writing. Interestingly, the decision to shut down the platform comes just a few months after Samsung announced a major update that introduced short-form videos from premium publishers like ABC News and USA Today.

Samsung News has undergone multiple rebrands since its launch. It debuted as Bixby Home in 2017 and became Samsung Daily in 2019. Just a year later, Samsung tried to relaunch its news hub again, this time as Samsung Free. None of these attempts ever succeeded in making the app all that popular among Galaxy users.

Samsung News launched in 2023 and may just prove to be Samsung's final attempt at a Google Discover rival before giving up for good. The latest versions of One UI already have Google Discover enabled by default anyway, so the Korean giant likely no longer sees a reason to put much effort into its own news aggregator. The news aggregator market is also facing tough times, with the increasing prominence of AI in services like Google Discover rapidly changing how people get news on their phones.

If true, Samsung News won't be the first One UI feature Samsung has replaced with a Google equivalent. In 2021, the company made Google Messages the default texting app instead of Samsung Messages. Then, in April 2026, Samsung officially discontinued Messages in the US, directing users to switch to Google Messages instead.

If you're a Samsung News user who's already received the shutdown notice or just want to get ahead of it, you can replace Samsung News with Google Discover. Press and hold any empty spot on the home screen, then swipe left and choose Google Discover instead of Samsung News. You can also turn off this news panel entirely. Instead of choosing between Google or Samsung, tap the settings icon at the top of this screen. Turn off the Media Page toggle, and you'll no longer see it on your phone.

Samsung notes that your preferences from its News platform won't carry over to other news aggregators, not even Google Discover. If you've been using Samsung News to follow specific publications, you'll have to follow each one again in whichever news app you use going forward. You'll want to remove the widgets from your home screen too, as they'll also stop working. While some will likely miss Samsung News, it also means there'll be one fewer app bloating your Galaxy phone.

#345. The haunting Masters meltdown that changed Rory McIlroy's career

Editor’s Note:  This story was originally published in April 2023.

Slumped on his club, head buried in his arm, Rory McIlroy looked on the verge of tears.

The then-21-year-old had just watched his ball sink into the waters of Rae’s Creek at Augusta National and with it, his dream of winning The Masters, a dream that had looked so tantalizingly close mere hours earlier.

As a four-time major winner and one of the most decorated names in the sport’s history, few players would turn down the chance to swap places with McIlroy heading into Augusta this week.

Yet on Sunday afternoon of April 10, 2011, not a golfer in the world would have wished to be in the Northern Irishman’s shoes.

A fresh-faced, mop-headed McIlroy had touched down in Georgia for the first major of the season with a reputation as the leading light of the next generation of stars.

An excellent 2010 had marked his best season since turning pro three years earlier, highlighted by a first PGA Tour win at the Quail Hollow Championship and a crucial contribution to Team Europe’s triumph at the Ryder Cup.

Yet despite a pair of impressive top-three finishes at the Open and PGA Championship respectively, a disappointing missed cut at The Masters – his first at a major – served as ominous foreshadowing.

McIlroy shot 74 and 77 to fall four strokes short of the cut line at seven-over par, a performance that concerned him enough to take a brief sabbatical from competition.

But one year on in 2011, any lingering Masters demons looked to have been exorcised as McIlroy flew round the Augusta fairways.

Having opened with a bogey-free seven-under 65 – the first time he had ever shot in the 60s at the major – McIlroy pulled ahead from Spanish first round co-leader Alvaro Quirós with a second round 69.

It sent him into the weekend holding a two-shot cushion over Australia’s Jason Day, with Tiger Woods a further stroke behind and back in the hunt for a 15th major after a surging second round 66.

And yet the 21-year-old leader looked perfectly at ease with having a target on his back. Even after a tentative start to the third round, McIlroy rallied with three birdies across the closing six holes to stretch his lead to four strokes heading into Sunday.

The youngster was out on his own ahead of a bunched chasing pack comprising Day, Ángel Cabrera, K.J. Choi and Charl Schwartzel. After 54 holes, McIlroy had shot just three bogeys.

“It’s a great position to be in … I’m finally feeling comfortable on this golf course,” McIlroy told reporters.

“I’m not getting ahead of myself, I know how leads can dwindle away very quickly. I have to go out there, not take anything for granted and go out and play as hard as I’ve played the last three days. If I can do that, hopefully things will go my way.

“We’ll see what happens tomorrow because four shots on this golf course isn’t that much.”

The truth can hurt, and McIlroy was about to prove his assessment of Augusta to be true in the most excruciating way imaginable.

His fourth bogey of the week arrived immediately. Having admitted to expecting some nerves at the first tee, McIlroy sparked a booming opening drive down the fairway, only to miss his putt from five feet.

Three consecutive pars steadied the ship, but Schwartzel had the wind in his sails. A blistering birdie, par, eagle start had seen him draw level at the summit after his third hole.

A subsequent bogey from the South African slowed his charge, as McIlroy clung onto a one-shot lead at the turn from Schwartzel, Cabrera, Choi, and a rampaging Woods, who shot five birdies and an eagle across the front nine to send Augusta into a frenzy.

Despite his dwindling advantage and the raucous Tiger-mania din ahead of him, McIlroy had responded well to another bogey at the 5th hole, draining a brilliant 20-foot putt at the 7th to restore his lead.

The fist pump that followed marked the high-water point of McIlroy’s round, as a sliding start accelerated into full-blown free-fall at the par-four 10th hole.

His tee shot went careening into a tree, ricocheting to settle between the white cabins that separate the main course from the adjacent par-three course. It offered viewers a glimpse at a part of Augusta rarely seen on broadcast, followed by pictures of McIlroy anxiously peering out from behind a tree to track his follow-up shot.

Though his initial escape was successful, yet another collision with a tree and a two-putt on the green saw a stunned McIlroy eventually tap in for a triple bogey. Having led the field one hole and seven shots earlier, he arrived at the 11th tee in seventh.

By the time his tee drive at the 13th plopped into the creek, all thoughts of who might be the recipient of the green jacket had long-since switched away from the anguished youngster. It had taken him seven putts to navigate the previous two greens, as a bogey and a double bogey dropped him to five-under – the score he had held after just 11 holes of the tournament.

Mercifully, the last five holes passed without major incident. A missed putt for birdie from five feet at the final hole summed up McIlroy’s day, though he was given a rousing reception as he left the green.

Mere minutes earlier, the same crowd had erupted as Schwartzel sunk his fourth consecutive birdie to seal his first major title. After starting the day four shots adrift of McIlroy, the South African finished 10 shots ahead of him, and two ahead of second-placed Australian duo Jason Day and Adam Scott.

McIlroy’s eight-over 80 marked the highest score of the round. Having headlined the leaderboard for most of the week, he finished tied-15th.

Tears would flow during a phone call with his parents the following morning, but at his press conference, McIlroy was upbeat.

“I’m very disappointed at the minute, and I’m sure I will be for the next few days, but I’ll get over it,” he said.

“I was leading this golf tournament with nine holes to go, and I just unraveled … It’s a Sunday at a major, what it can do.

“This is my first experience at it, and hopefully the next time I’m in this position I’ll be able to handle it a little better. I didn’t handle it particularly well today obviously, but it was a character-building day … I’ll come out stronger for it.”

Once again, McIlroy would be proven right.

Just eight weeks later in June, McIlroy rampaged to an eight-shot victory at the US Open. Records tumbled in his wake at Congressional, as he shot a tournament record 16-under 268 to become the youngest major winner since Tiger Woods at The Masters in 1997.

The historic victory kickstarted a golden era for McIlroy. After coasting to another eight-shot win at the PGA Championship in 2012, McIlroy became only the third golfer since 1934 to win three majors by the age of 25 with triumph at the 2014 Open Championship.

Before the year was out, he would add his fourth major title with another PGA Championship win.

And much of it was owed to that fateful afternoon at Augusta. In an interview with the BBC in 2015, McIlroy dubbed it “the most important day” of his career.

“If I had not had the whole unravelling, if I had just made a couple of bogeys coming down the stretch and lost by one, I would not have learned as much.

“Luckily, it did not take me long to get into a position like that again when I was leading a major and I was able to get over the line quite comfortably. It was a huge learning curve for me and I needed it, and thankfully I have been able to move on to bigger and better things.

“Looking back on what happened in 2011, it doesn’t seem as bad when you have four majors on your mantelpiece.”

McIlroy’s contentment came with a caveat: it would be “unthinkable” if he did not win The Masters in his career.

Yet as he prepares for his 15th appearance at Augusta National this week, a green jacket remains an elusive missing item from his wardrobe.

Despite seven top-10 finishes in his past 10 Masters outings, the trophy remains the only thing separating McIlroy from joining the ranks of golf immortals to have completed golf’s career grand slam of all four majors in the modern era: Gene Sarazen, Ben Hogan, Gary Player, Jack Nicklaus, and Tiger Woods.

A runner-up finish to Scottie Scheffler last year marked McIlroy’s best finish at Augusta, yet arguably 2011 remains the closest he has ever been to victory. A slow start in 2022 meant McIlroy had begun Sunday’s deciding round 10 shots adrift of the American, who teed off for his final hole with a five-shot lead despite McIlroy’s brilliant 64 finish.

At 33 years old, time is still on his side. Though 2022 extended his major drought to eight years, it featured arguably his best golf since that golden season in 2014.

And as McIlroy knows better than most, things can change quickly at Augusta National.

#344. Checking your Apple Watch's battery health is easier than you think

It just takes a couple of clicks and taps.

At 50 hours of normal use on a single charge and 84 hours in low power mode, the new Apple Watch Ultra 4's battery life is eye-popping, but nothing lasts forever.

Whether it's an iPhone, iPad or Apple Watch, any device's lithium-ion batteries get weaker as they age. This leads to less time between charging sessions, less overall battery capacity and generally worse performance.

Although Apple says every model starting from the Series 5, SE and Ultra has software that reduces the risk of poor performance in these cases, you should still keep an eye on your battery health. So whether you ultimately decide to replace it or buy a whole new watch, these are the steps you need to take to check the health of your battery.

Checking your Apple Watch's battery status is simple. Go to Settings > Battery > Battery Health. Here, you can activate optimized battery charging and learn about your maximum battery capacity. A lower capacity will likely lead to fewer hours of use before you need to charge it. Similar to an iPhone, making a trip to the Genius Bar might be needed once the Apple Watch battery's max capacity dips below 80%.

Luckily, if you don't keep a close eye on it in the settings menu, you will still get an alert letting you know when the battery requires service.

As for the optimization feature, it is supported on models as old as the Series 6, Apple Watch SE and the first Ultra. Turning it on charges the device based on your typical charging habits to improve the lifespan. It also delays charging over 80%, keeping the battery level between 75% and 80%. The goal is for it to be fully charged by the time you remove it.

Beyond updating your device to the latest watchOS, you can take other steps to preserve an Apple Watch's battery life. For starters, turn on Low Power Mode to deactivate oxygen monitoring, always-on display, and other features you might not really use, which drain your battery in the background.

When tracking a run or walk, disabling the heart rate sensor can help in the long run; turn on Power Saving Mode under the Workout section in the iPhone's Apple Watch app. While it might lead to some inaccurate health metrics, it'll help preserve the battery's health.

You can also disable features like Wake on Wrist Raise for preservation. Press the Digital Crown, then head to Settings > Display & Brightness and scroll down to Wake. From there, you can turn it on or off. You can also do this temporarily by turning on Theater Mode, which will prevent the screen from turning on whenever you make a slight move or raise your wrist.

#341. What does an NPU do and why do so many laptops have them?

Bought a new laptop recently? Chances are that it's equipped with an NPU, a chip you're almost certainly not using. The NPU, or Neural Processing Unit, is a block of silicon that runs AI workloads at a fraction of the power a CPU or GPU needs. Roughly 2W compared to well over 100W that standard laptop discrete graphics need to do the same job. While they're not yet found in all laptops, they're now pretty much standard in mid-range and premium machines.

Advisory firm Gartner reckons that AI-capable PCs, like these NPU-equipped laptops, make up more than half of total global shipments. The reason we're seeing this isn't because buyers want or need them, but to align with certification requirements. Back in 2024, Microsoft pretty much dictated that laptop makers will need to hit 40 TOPS (the measure of how quickly an NPU can chew through AI math) of dedicated NPU performance with new machines, or risk losing access to new Windows AI features. NPU hardware is now flying off the shelves as a result, but software is lagging behind.

An NPU's job is to accelerate inference. That's the "run this model" phase rather than the GPU-powered "train this model" phase. Neural networks rely heavily on two kinds of computation to do this: matrix multiplication and nonlinear activation functions. NPUs are purpose-built to execute those operations as quickly and efficiently as possible, but that comes at the cost of some general-purpose CPU and GPU flexibility.

Let's consider the example of using background blur on a video call. Most of us have used this, and it can run on either a CPU or GPU. But both draw a lot of power, generating heat and sapping battery life on a thin portable. An NPU performs the same work using a fraction of the energy, so features like webcam effects can run continuously without draining the battery or spinning up fans.

NPUs are obviously no good for training AI models, and to run large local LLMs like Llama 70B, you'll still need a discrete GPU with a decent chunk of video memory. They're also not needed for services like ChatGPT or Gemini because those run on provider infrastructure. Their actual use case, at least for now, is a small number of always-on and low-power use cases like webcam effects, noise suppression, real-time translation and local search indexing.

The reason we're seeing so many laptops featuring NPUs is because of Microsoft's Copilot + PC certification. Laptop makers can only earn it and unlock certain on-device Windows AI features if their laptops have a 40 TOPS NPU, plus 16GB of RAM and 256GB of storage. That 40 TOPS figure also has to come from the NPU, not a GPU; a mid-range laptop RTX 4050 offers north of 190 TOPS from its tensor cores. That doesn't count.

Qualcomm's Snapdragon X Elite and Plus chips were the first to market with a 45 TOPS Hexagon NPU. That was soon followed by Intel's Lunar Lake with up to 48 TOPS, and AMD's Ryzen AI 300 at 50 TOPS. Intel's newer Panther Lake processors, known as Core Ultra Series 3, come with a 50 NPU TOPS on Intel's 18A process. Later this year, Qualcomm has since pushed that to as much as 85 TOPS with Snapdragon X2 Elite, more than double Microsoft's specified minimum. Every generation has ratcheted the number higher even though software to consume those TOPS remains scarce. Soon, AI laptops may well be the only option available, making NPUs unavoidable. We've already seen Dell stuff an enterprise-grade NPU into its Pro Max Plus laptop.

If you've got an NPU-equipped laptop, you can see its utilization rate via Task Manager on Windows 11. On my laptop — a 2024 ASUS Zenbook Duo UX8406 in a 32GB RAM configuration — this sits at zero, and I'd imagine that to be the case on all casual user machines.

Alas, the list of apps that lean on the NPU remains short: Windows Studio Effects, Live Captions, Recall and Click to Do, Teams and Zoom noise suppression and a handful of Adobe Creative Cloud features.

To see how much of my 34 TOPS Intel AI Boost NPU a local model would hog, I downloaded Mistral 7B, a fairly decent, efficient open-source model and ran it via Intel's OpenVINO toolkit. I then asked it to generate 2,500 words on neural processing units.

Although my machine has 34 platform TOPS combined across the CPU, GPU and NPU, only 11 are dedicated to the NPU. Mistral 7B pegged the NPU at 98 percent while the CPU sat at three percent. Text generation worked, and while 11 TOPS doesn't leave much headroom for a model of that size, my laptop remained fast and responsive.

You can see how this compares to running the same local model off the NPU using Ollama. CPU utilization jumped to 52 percent with memory use holding at around 17GB of my 32GB capacity. If I were running other CPU-intensive workloads, my laptop would've ground to a halt. That's the point of an NPU: It handles an AI workload without impacting the rest of the system. But it required a specific toolkit and technical knowledge to get there in this instance; very little software natively supports it.

#338. In reversal, American Cancer Society urges routine prostate cancer screening

Men aged 50–69 and at average risk should get PSA screening every two years.

In a significant update to its guidelines for prostate cancer screening, the American Cancer Society is now recommending that men get routinely screened for prostate cancer with a PSA (prostate-specific antigen) test.

Men at average risk should get a PSA test every two years from age 50 to 69, according to the new guidelines released Thursday.

Men considered at high risk due to race and family history should start testing earlier, at 45, and most are recommended to get tested every year. Specifically, yearly testing starting at age 45 is recommended for all Black men, who have higher rates of prostate cancer. Non-Black men should also get yearly testing starting at 45 if a close relative was diagnosed with prostate cancer before age 65, or if more than one of their relatives has had prostate cancer. On the other hand, if only one close relative was diagnosed with prostate cancer and it was diagnosed at age 65 or older, non-Black men in this case should start PSA screening at 45, but are recommended to get testing only every two years.

Men ages 70 to 74 should consult their doctor on continuing screening, while those 75 and up are not recommended to get screened.

The new guidance departs from ACS’s previous iteration, published in 2010, which made no universal recommendations for routine screening. Men at age 50 were recommended to use shared-decision making with their doctors on whether or not to get tested. The recommendation was similar to that from the US Preventive Services Task Force, a federal panel that regularly evaluates evidence and makes recommendations on such preventive medical care. (The USPSTF is currently working on an update to its prostate cancer screening recommendation, though it should be noted that the panel has recently been overhauled by anti-vaccine Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and new members are reportedly rife with conflicts of interest.)

In announcing the guidelines today, the ACS says its updates are based on new evidence since 2010 that shows screening saves lives, and that advances in case management can avoid the concerning harms from overdiagnosis and overtreatment. For many men with prostate cancer, their cancer will never grow or cause harm in their lifetime, while treatment can run the risk of erectile dysfunction and urinary incontinence.

In the new guidance, the ACS adds guardrails, firstly advising all men to be informed about the risks and benefits. If a PSA test comes back high—defined as 3 ng/mL or higher for men under 70 and 6.5 ng/mL or higher for those 70 and up—the ACS recommends repeating the test before taking any next steps.

If repeat testing is still high, then men should get either a prostate MRI or a validated biomarker test to assess risk. Only if there is a high suspicion of cancer—such as having a very high PSA test result—should men jump to a prostate biopsy.

For men diagnosed with prostate cancer, active surveillance should be the initial management strategy for men whose cancer appears to be at low risk of growing or spreading.

“By catching aggressive cancers with a simple PSA blood test, you open the door to highly effective treatments that protect your future,” Dr. Shanthi Sivendran, interim chief patient officer for the ACS, said in a statement. “Meanwhile, lower-risk findings can be safely managed through careful, active surveillance.”

Prostate cancer is one of the most common cancers in men and the second leading cause of cancer death in US men, the ACS notes. Nearly 334,00 men are estimated to be diagnosed with prostate cancer in 2026, and it’s estimated that over 36,320 will die from the disease.

This post was updated for clarity on November 12.

#336. How to check which iOS version your iPhone is running

Apple's products may not always offer the best bang for your buck — the company still sells an iPhone with a 60Hz display for $700, for example — but they often make up for it with meticulously designed hardware and well-thought-out ecosystem features. iPhones also tend to last a long time, with Apple's commitment to long-term software support a major factor. Take the iPhone 11, for instance. Released in 2019, it can still run the latest version of iOS more than seven years later. If you're rocking a similarly aged iPhone and want to check the OS version you're running, open Settings and navigate to General > About > iOS Version.

Your iPhone should notify you when a new iOS version becomes available, and installation takes only a few minutes once the update finishes downloading. To check for updates manually, navigate to Settings > General > Software Update. This page also shows the current software version and will display a Download and Install button if an update is available. If a major iOS release, like iOS 27, is available, you'll see it in a separate Also Available section at the bottom.

Once you've downloaded the update, tap Update Now, enter your passcode and accept the terms and conditions. Your iPhone will reboot automatically to finish installing the update. You can also configure your iPhone to download and install iOS updates automatically. Tap on Automatic Updates and turn the Automatically Install toggle on. Your iPhone will handle software updates on its own when it's connected to Wi-Fi and has enough battery left. For manual updates, your battery needs to have at least 20 percent charge.

Update sizes vary depending on the type of release. Security updates and hotfixes may only be a couple hundred megabytes, while major iOS upgrades can be several gigabytes, so you should connect to a fast Wi-Fi network if you're downloading the latter. If your Wi-Fi is spotty or unreliable, you can also update to the latest iOS version via a computer.

Start by connecting your iPhone to your computer with a cable. You might need to tap Trust on your iPhone's screen if it's your first time connecting it to that computer. If you're using a Mac running macOS 10.15 or newer, open Finder and select your iPhone from the sidebar. In the General tab, click on Check for Update, then confirm by clicking on Update. If you have a Windows PC, you can install the Apple Devices app to update your iPhone. You can still use iTunes on an older Mac or Windows computer, too.

Though iOS updates rarely have catastrophic issues, Apple recommends backing up your iPhone before installing software updates. On your iPhone, open Settings, tap on your name at the top, navigate to iCloud > iCloud Backup and Back Up Now. If you're out of iCloud storage, you can back up your iPhone to a Mac or Windows PC using Finder, iTunes or the Apple Devices app.

It's a running joke in the tech community that Apple keeps releasing the same iPhone every year. iOS also refrains from making drastic changes from one generation to the next, although iOS 26's Liquid Glass overhaul was pretty big. iOS 27 doesn't look too different from its predecessor, but it packs significantly better performance. This is especially noticeable on older iPhone models: My iPhone 15 Pro was very sluggish on iOS 26, but iOS 27 brought major stability and performance improvements.

Both iOS 18 and iOS 26 were infamous for being buggy and not delivering on Apple's promises about a smarter Siri, so it's understandable if you've held back on updating your older iPhone. iOS 27, though, is one of the more polished releases, likely because it prioritizes stability over introducing flashy new features. iOS 26 was particularly demanding on older iPhones, but iOS 27 improves the experience with a new optimized CPU scheduler and can launch apps up to 30 percent faster, according to Apple.

Siri AI is also finally here, and users with Apple Intelligence-powered iPhones can join the beta waitlist by heading to Settings > Siri. It's still far from the ultra-capable AI assistant that Apple originally hinted at during its WWDC 2024 event, but it's noticeably better at fulfilling requests and handling more complex, conversational commands. Of course, software updates also patch security issues and vulnerabilities, which is just as important, if not more so, than any new features.

#335. Common reasons your PC's camera and microphone aren't working

It's an annoying problem but one that can be easily fixed

The webcams on our PCs are essential pieces of equipment. There's a chance you conducted an interview for your most recent job with one, and even major news outlets regularly talk to experts or pundits this way instead of inviting them down to the studio. It helps that cams have gone from choppy and muffled feeds to something closer to broadcast quality, and of course professionals often use dedicated equipment.

Everyone runs into problems, though, and we're here to tackle them as efficiently as possible. Often the fixes are simple, maybe even simpler than you'd expect. But there can be more complicated issues at play, for instance requiring driver updates.

If you're on the verge of an important call or meeting, we can probably get you back on track in a matter of minutes. But whenever possible, we'd recommend testing and adjusting gear during downtime, because the goal is to get audio and video just right, rather than merely working.

This might almost feel insulting, but your first step should be to verify that your equipment isn't physically disabled. Some computers have lens blinds and/or mute switches, and it's easy to forget about them if you don't take that many calls. If you're using external accessories, check their own cables, switches and buttons.

Your next step should be to make sure Windows or macOS has the proper input(s) selected, and that mic volume is high enough. In Windows 11, you can check your camera by heading to Settings > Bluetooth & devices > Camera, and mic input via Settings > System > Sound. As a rule, err on the side of mic volume being high, meaning 80 to 100 percent — I've found that even with headset mics, low volume is usually the culprit for people being unable to hear you. Macs use app-based camera controls, but you can adjust mic input through Apple menu > System Settings > Sound > Input.

It's also vital to make sure your inputs and volume are properly selected within the settings menus of the apps you're using. And even when they are configured properly, some meeting apps may nevertheless default to leaving one or more inputs disabled. With Zoom, for example, be sure to doublecheck that camera and/or mic input is allowed in the prompt that appears before you join a meeting.

If you're still encountering trouble, it may be time to check for software updates using Settings > Windows Update or, on Macs, Apple menu > System Settings > General > Software Update. Note that while Windows Update breaks out driver releases, these are bundled into new versions of macOS, so you won't necessarily be able to tell what's changed. Both Mac and Windows users should update to the latest versions of any relevant communications apps and features.

On the Windows side, you may want to update your GPU drivers via AMD or NVIDIA's software if you're encountering weird or missing video output, although this is more likely to affect how things look on your end, not someone else's. As a last-ditch measure, open Device Manager by searching for it in the taskbar, then expand the Cameras or Audio inputs and outputs sections to find your hardware. If you right-click on a device, select Properties and click on the Driver tab, you'll get an option to uninstall. Windows should automatically reinstall drivers once you reboot. If it doesn't, you may have to manually identify the correct drivers via a manufacturer's website and download them.

#334. Judge Allows Trump’s Defamation Lawsuit Against the BBC to Proceed

President Trump is seeking damages from the British broadcaster over a documentary it conceded was misleadingly edited.

A federal judge in Florida on Tuesday allowed President Trump’s defamation lawsuit against the BBC to proceed, rejecting the British broadcaster’s bid to dismiss it.

Mr. Trump sued the BBC over its documentary “Trump: A Second Chance?” which aired a week before the 2024 presidential election. The program spliced together two portions of remarks that Mr. Trump delivered roughly 55 minutes apart on Jan. 6, 2021, giving the impression that he was encouraging his supporters to storm the U.S. Capitol.

Mr. Trump’s legal team has accused the BBC of “intentionally, maliciously and deceptively doctoring his speech” in an effort to interfere with the election, and is seeking $10 billion in damages.

The BBC has apologized, acknowledging that its editing gave “the mistaken impression that Trump made a direct call for violent action,” a controversy that prompted the resignations of its director general, Tim Davie, and news chief, Deborah Turness. But it says it was not evidence of a fundamental bias in the BBC’s news reporting and did not constitute defamation.

On Truth Social, Mr. Trump described Tuesday’s ruling as a “A Huge Victory against Fake News BBC.”

A spokeswoman for the BBC said in an emailed statement: “We are surprised by this decision but respect the court’s authority and note the case will now proceed to the next stage. We remain confident in our position and will continue to respond through the proper legal process.”

Lawyers for the BBC had sought to have the lawsuit dismissed, in part because the program was never aired in the United States.

#333. Specialized’s Tarmac SL9 S-Level is built to wreck your Zone 2 ride

Specialized’s second-fastest bike may be the smart buy.

I love a good Zone 2 ride. There’s nothing like getting on the bike, settling into a groove, and letting the miles (and hours) flow by. But sometimes when I hopped on the Specialized Tarmac SL9 S-Level, Zone 2 would turn into a tempo ride. It was like having a little imp—the stereotype dressed in red with the pitchfork—on my left shoulder whispering into my ear: “Go fast. This bike was built to go fast. Speed is good. You can do a Zone 2 ride tomorrow.” Normally, I’d count on the good imp—the dude with the harp and wings—on my right shoulder to restrain these urges. But the Tarmac is so seductive that he would just shrug and say “he’s got a point.” And in a moment of weakness, I would drop the hammer and head into the red, just because the SL9 makes that so rewarding.

The Tarmac SL9 is Specialized’s aero road bike, with the S-Level sitting just below the S-Works in Specialized’s top tier of carbon, aero road bikes, where it replaced the Tarmac SL8 Pro. After it got an update this year, I spent several weeks riding it, putting nearly 1,000 miles on it

Specialized offers the Tarmac SL9 in four models, all available with SRAM and Shimano drivetrains (Ars tested the SRAM version). Notably, you don’t need to buy the top-of-the-line bike to get the top-of-the-line groupset. Here’s the breakdown of the Tarmac SL9 lineup (note that the Shimano versions of the Expert is 20 g lighter and Comp is 70 grams heavier than the SRAM versions):

The $10,500 S-Level offers the top-of-the-line SRAM Red groupset and integrated cockpit, just like the $14,000 S-Works. But the frameset, wheelset, and saddle differ. The major difference is the frame: the S-Level gets the same carbon-fiber FACT 10r frame as the Expert and Comp. At 822 g for a 56 cm frame, the FACT 10r is 135 g heavier than the FACT 12r used on the S-Works. Despite the weight difference, Specialized says the FACT 10r offers the same stiffness and comfort characteristics as its lighter sibling. Along with the frame, different wheelsets and saddles make the S-Level 500 g heavier than the S-Works. With bottle cages, a Garmin mount, and my preferred Shimano XTR XC PD-M9200 MTB pedals, the S-Level I tested weighed in at 7.98 kg. By way of comparison, my own road bike—a Gen 8 Trek Madone—weighs in at 7.71 kg.

I rode the S-Level all around the Chicago suburbs as well as in central Illinois. Unlike the Diverge 4 Pro, I wasn’t able to test its climbing ability in the Rocky Mountains. All we’ve got in most of Illinois are short, punchy climbs … and a lot of long flats. I rode The S-Level on everything from freshly laid asphalt to freshly laid chipseal, including a couple of 60-mile-plus rides on the country roads downstate.

Visually, the S-Level is striking. The blue-on-white with gray striping is one of Specialized’s better-looking colorways. And it looks aerodynamic. Indeed, Specialized says the Tarmac SL9 is the most aerodynamic road bike it has ever made. Notable changes from the previous-generation Tarmac SL8 to SL9 involved tweaking the head tube, rerouting the rear hydraulic brake hose to accommodate the narrower head tube, and moving to a dropped-down tube for improved aerodynamics. But the most visually striking change is the Win Fin. As the seat tube rises from the bottom bracket, it deviates from the vertical to follow the curve of the wheel as it approaches the seat stays. When riding with just a single water bottle on the downtube—common in pro races where a full bottle is just a team car away—Specialized claims Win Fin saves riders half a watt.

The S-Level I tested came with Specialized’s 30 mm Specialized Cotton TLR tires—used by Red Bull-BORA-hansgrohe on the UCI World Tour—in a tubeless setup. According to Bicycle Rolling Resistance, the Cotton TLR outperforms the much-loved Continental GP 5000 S TR tires when it comes to rolling resistance (at 28 mm). Using Silca’s tire pressure calculator, I rode with the tires inflated to 73 psi in the front and 75 psi in the rear, a departure from the 62/64 setting on my 32 mm Contis—and there is a slight, but noticeable difference in ride comfort between the S-Level and my own road bike. Mounted on the Roval Rapide CL III carbon wheels with 21 mm internal width, the Cotton TLR tires measured 30.2 mm wide (my 32 mm Contis are a hair over 33 mm).

On every surface shy of brand-new chipseal, the Tarmac felt comfortable and balanced, with the bike absorbing some of the punishment meted out by uneven pavement. Fresh chipseal is another matter entirely, as it feels more like gravel, which felt jarring on the SL9 S-Level. What was particularly impressive about the SL9 is how great it feels on long rides. Some manufacturers are skilled at building aero bikes that feel great on hours-long rides, and the Tarmac is just as good as the Trek Madone SLR 9 AXS Gen 8 I reviewed in this regard.

When you’re ready to drop the hammer, the S-Level is your willing accomplice. It’s twitchy in all of the good ways, with instantaneous response to the rider’s effort. The SRAM Red AXS groupset makes shifting buttery smooth (and the bonus buttons on the brake hoods allow the rider to change screens on the bike computer without releasing the brake hoods), and the drivetrain (50t/37t chainrings and a 10t-36t cassette) offers gear ratios for every type of terrain.

The first few seconds of a climb on the Tarmac SL9 S-Level feel like they come for free. Whether I stayed seated or cranked out watts in an upright position, there was no lag or flex as the bike snapped forward. Descents were amazing, and cornering on the S-Level is sublime—I felt balanced and in control at all times.

There are a few nits to pick. The reach to the brakes in the drops felt excessive on my first couple of rides, and I had to adjust them slightly to brake easily on descents. Also, I would prefer shorter cranks on the Tarmac. The trend among professional riders has been toward shorter cranks because it makes holding an aero position easier and reduces hip and knee flexion. To its credit, Specialized reduced the crank length from 172.5 mm on the 56 cm SL8 to 170 mm on the same-sized SL9, but I run 165 mm cranks on my road bikes and noticed the difference on the S-Level. One demographic that buys expensive road bikes is middle-aged dudes with empty nests and disposable incomes, and they are the ones most likely to appreciate shorter cranks.

The 3D-printed Power Pro Mirror is a fine saddle, but there’s a reason I ride with a Specialized S-Works Power with Mirror on my Trek—it’s more comfortable and offers noticeably more padding around the cutout. And if I owned the S-Level, I’d move to 32 mm tires as soon as I wore out the 30s for better compliance.

Specialized brags that the Tarmac SL9 S-Works is the fastest bike ever made, and it claims the S-Level is the second-fastest bike ever made. I can’t speak to that claim, but the SL9 S-Level checks all of the boxes for an aerodynamic road bike. It’s lightweight, it’s fast, it’s responsive, and it’s great on rollers and punchy climbs. And it’s nice to get a SRAM Red groupset without springing for the absolute top-of-the-line model. $10,500 is a hefty sum for a road bike, but I’d be a lot more willing to forego the weight savings from the lighter components (frame, wheels, seatpost, bottom bracket, and bearings) of the S-Works—and spend $3,500 less. The real selling point, though, is how often it made me want to go harder just for the fun of it. That little imp has a point: Zone 2 can wait until tomorrow.

#331. Angel Reese defends gesture directed towards Caitlin Clark after LSU national title win; calls out double standard after being 'unapologetically' her

LSU star Angel Reese defended the gesture she aimed at Iowa Hawkeyes’ Caitlin Clark near the end of the Tigers’ first NCAA women’s basketball national championship victory on Sunday, saying “I don’t take disrespect lightly.”

Reese could be seen approaching Clark before moving her open hand in front of her face – popularized by WWE star John Cena to mean “you can’t see me” – before pointing to her ring finger in a gesture some interpreted as a reference to the place her newly-acquired championship ring might sit.

Caitlin Clark breaks records galore during historic March Madness run

Clark made a similar gesture to another player earlier in the tournament.

The gesture has sparked much debate, especially on social media. Some have criticized Reese, while others have defended her actions, highlighting how there was no public outrage in response to Clark’s gesture earlier in the tournament.

Sports journalist Jose de Jesus Ortiz called Reese’s actions “classless,” while former ESPN host Keith Olbermann called Reese an “idiot” for the gesture.

In the press conference after the victory, Reese referenced the difference in reaction she received as a result of her gesture as compared to the one Clark received.

“All year, I was critiqued for who I was. I don’t fit the narrative,” Reese said. “I don’t fit the box that y’all want me to be in. I’m too hood. I’m too ghetto. Y’all told me that all year. But when other people do it, and y’all don’t say nothing.

“So this is for the girls that look like me. For those that want to speak up for what they believe in. It’s unapologetically you. And that’s what I did it for tonight. It was bigger than me tonight. And Twitter is going to go into a rage every time.

“And I’m happy. I feel like I’ve helped grow women’s basketball this year. (…) I’m looking forward to celebrating and then next season.”

LSU beats Iowa to win its first NCAA women's basketball championship

Reese had 15 points and 10 rebounds in the 102-85 victory and won the women’s March Madness’ Most Outstanding Player award.

In the post-game broadcast, Reese referenced the similar gesture Clark made to a Louisville opponent in the Elite Eight.

In the same game, Clark said to an opponent: “You’re down by 15 points. Shut up,” according to the Bleacher Report.

“Caitlin Clark is a hell of a player but I don’t take disrespect lightly,” Reese said. “She disrespected [LSU’s] Alexis [Morris] (…) and I wanted to pick her pocket. But I had a moment at the end of her game. I was in my bag, I was in my moment.”

After the Championship game, Clark herself said she didn’t notice anything at the time.

“I was just trying to get to the handshake line and shake hands and be grateful that my team was in that position,” Clark said in the post-game press conference. “All the credit in the world to LSU. They were tremendous. They deserve it. They had a tremendous season.

“(LSU head coach) Kim Mulkey coached them so, so well. She’s one of the best basketball coaches of all time, and it shows. She only said really kind things to me in the handshake line, so I’m very grateful of that too.

“But honestly I have no idea. I was just trying to spend the last few moments on the court with especially the five people that I’ve started 93 games with and relishing every second of that.”

LSU head coach Mulkey said she had “no clue” about what transpired.

Among those defending Reese on social media were ESPN’s Holly Rowe and former NBA star Etan Thomas.

“People hating on Angel Reese or Caitlin Clark. Stop. Unapologetically confident young women should be celebrated NOT hated. Get used to it,” Rowe wrote on Twitter.

Former Washington Wizards, Oklahoma City Thunder and Atlanta Hawks player Thomas wrote: “Hold on now!!!! It was cute when Caitlin Clark did it. Y’all didn’t have any issues with it at all. So don’t be all outraged and talking about class and sportsmanship when Angel Reese does the same thing. We’re not doing double standards here.”

Reese said the negative reaction on social media throughout the season has helped fuel her excellent season, having finished averaging 23.0 points and 15.4 rebounds in her first season with LSU after transferring from Maryland.

“Twitter can say what they want to say,” she said. “I love reading those comments. I have all the screenshots of what everybody has said about me all season. What are you going to say now?”

#330. Your Apple AirPods Pro can test your hearing in five minutes, but are they accurate?

Your Apple AirPods Pro Can Test Your Hearing in Five Minutes, But Is It Accurate?

With active noise-canceling and solid sound quality, Apple AirPods Pro are some of the best earbuds you can pair with your iPhone, but they can do a lot more than deliver great sound. No matter your age, it's important to do what you can to slow or prevent hearing loss, and AirPods Pro may actually be able to help with that. AirPods Pro 2 and 3 models have built-in hearing test and hearing aid features that are worth looking into, whether you think you're experiencing hearing loss or not.

The hearing test feature arrived in October 2024 along with iOS 18.1. It's touted by Apple as a "clinical-grade" test and can be completed in as little as five minutes. Given that commercially available health devices like heart rate monitors can vary widely in how effective they are, there's good reason to doubt just how good the AirPods Pro's hearing test could actually be. While it's no replacement for seeing an audiologist, the evidence shows that Apple's hearing test can deliver accurate results under the right conditions.

To even release the hearing test and hearing aid features, Apple had to receive FDA authorization. That process involved a clinical study of the hearing aid features specifically, but the hearing test has also been the subject of studies after release. A 2026 study by an international team of researchers published in Otolaryngology–Head and Neck Surgery found that the AirPods Pro showed "clinically acceptable accuracy and reliability" when compared against a standard audiometry test. The study also pointed out that Apple's hearing test is much faster and easier to perform than an in-office exam, which could lead to more people actually taking their hearing health seriously.

However, that doesn't mean your AirPods Pro hearing health tools can substitute for a doctor's visit. Apple's hearing test is considered a valid screening tool, but it can't provide a diagnosis — only a doctor can do that. It's also a much more limited screening than a doctor can provide. The AirPods Pro hearing test is based on "pure-tone audiometry", which measures how clearly you perceive different sound frequencies. A visit to the audiologist would include additional tests to measure bone conduction and eardrum health, which give a fuller picture of your hearing and can tell you the cause of hearing loss. It's also important to note that studies so far have been small, so while their results are compelling, they're still limited.

Getting an accurate reading from the AirPods Pro also means taking the hearing test under the right conditions. The AirPods need to form a complete seal in your ears, and finding ear tips that fit properly can sometimes be difficult. You also need to take the test in a quiet environment without a lot of background noise. The test itself will alert you if it detects too much noise around you or a poor in-ear fit, but taking a test at a doctor's office will always be more reliable.

The AirPods Pro test is intended only to screen for normal hearing loss of the kind that everyone experiences to some degree as we age. If your hearing suddenly gets worse, you have ear pain or hearing is worse in one ear than the other, you should see a doctor as soon as possible. That makes Apple's hearing test a great place to start before you're experiencing hearing loss symptoms, not a solution once they appear.

#329. 5 excellent free Apple Watch apps every owner should know about

Plenty of watch apps are free to download and then put all wrist-related features behind a paywall. These ones don’t.

So you've just strapped on a new Apple Watch, paired it with your iPhone and opened up the App Store to fill it up with cool software. Plenty of what you'll find there says it's free, and most of it is — right up until you try to use the component that runs on your wrist. The App Store explains that apps marked with Get instead of a price tag can still come with in-app purchases, and that's often where the paywall is with watch apps.

Let's take Spotify as an example. Its free tier will refuse to play anything from the watch at all, allowing those on the free tier to only control music playing on another device. Meanwhile, Pocket Casts (a cross-platform podcast player) locks standalone watch playback behind its $39.99/year Plus Plan. Fitness apps commonly do this, too, with hiking route planner Footpath putting its watch features behind a paid tier, and Komoot forcing new users to pay for Premium before they can send a route to a device.

In response, we've put together a short list of great apps where the main Apple Watch functionality is completely free to use. All five of these apps run on watchOS 27 (which Apple released in September 2026 along with iOS 27, macOS Golden Gate and other major OS updates). They work on the Apple Watch Series 9, Ultra 2, SE 3 and anything newer.

If you're obsessed with tracking your steps, there's no better free-to-use app than Pedometer++. It's made and maintained by indie dev David Smith, who redesigned the entire watch app for version 8 back in April. Access to its core features is completely free, including a running step count, complications for your watch face, and the option to start and track indoor or outdoor walks, runs and hikes from your wrist. This all syncs with Apple Health.

There's a Premium option (and it truly is optional), which will set you back $3.99 per month or $29.99 per year. For that, you get maps on the watch, offline maps for workouts, Live Activities on your iPhone's lock screen and something called Expedition Mode, which cuts back on constant heart rate tracking to stretch battery life by up to 40 percent, according to Smith. While you don't need Premium to count steps or log a walk, the free version does show ads.

Nike Run Club doesn't have any paid tiers or in-app purchases at all; the watch app has been able to track a run without your phone since 2019. It puts Nike's audio-coached Guided Runs, always-on stats, live pace charts and streak badges on your wrist, along with a Nike watch face that moves with you. If you've got a cellular Apple Watch, a 2026 update also lets you share your live location during a run.

So if you want a coached running app that won't ask you for money at any point, Nike Run Club is the one to get.

You're probably aware that Whoop's bands come with a (virtually) mandatory subscription, the cheapest of which is currently $199 per year. Bevel is Apple Watch's answer to Whoop that takes the data your watch is already collecting and turns it into the same kind of daily recovery, sleep, strain and stress scores you'd get with the screenless wearable, all for free. On top of that, with Bevel, you also get nutrition tracking, strength training logs, cycle tracking, and journal along with the Apple Watch app, widgets and complications.

It was only fairly recently that Bevel made most of that free, back in December 2025. Bevel Pro is still around and adds an AI health coach, health records, a biological age estimate and training plans for $14.99 per month, or $99.99 per year. However, on the Apple Watch itself, the App Store listing for Bevel only talks about strength workouts, which sync between your wrist and your phone. The scores are built from heart rate, HRV and sleep data your watch collects in the background.

If you use Spotify or Pocket Casts and want to play your podcasts from your watch, you'll have to pay to do so. But there's a free alternative: Overcast. Its App Store listing promises standalone playback and cellular streaming on the watch, while its core app is free and supported by non-intrusive ads for other shows (with an optional subscription to get rid of them). With Overcast, you can download podcasts ahead of time and play them on the go, even if you've left your phone behind. It's a basic app done very well.

Unlike most large podcast apps, Overcast is maintained by a single developer. In fact, the dev rewrote the watch app from scratch last year to make it faster and more reliable. A slew of updates have been added since then, including Double Tap for play and pause, Smart Speed, and Voice Boost to download episodes. Smart Speed works by trimming silences out of episodes, while Voice Boost evens out quiet voices so podcasts on your wrist now sound the same as they would on your phone.

However, it's worth noting that streaming over cellular will eat into your battery. The Apple Watch uses the least amount of power when it's connected to your phone via Bluetooth, while Wi-Fi connections use less power than cellular. Weak signals also drain the battery faster, as does playing audio through the watch's speaker rather than a pair of headphones. In other words, when using Overcast from your wrist, download shows first and listen via AirPods for best results.

I used Overcast to play the latest episode of The Common Descent Podcast by David Moscato and Will Harris while walking my dog, streamed via cellular on my Watch Ultra 3 and connected my AirPods Max 2. I have zero issues to report from that experience.

Shazam needs no introduction as the beloved music ID utility. If you've noticed that it disappeared from your watch, you'll now find it as a separate, watch-only app called Shazam Music Recognition. Apple develops it, it's free with no in-app purchases and needs watchOS 11 or later. Shazam's history also syncs with iCloud, so anything you tag on your watch will show up in the app on your iPhone.

You can install all five of these apps from the App Store on the watch itself, or via the Watch app on your iPhone under My Watch > Available Apps. Before you download anything, though, check what the watch app does without a subscription, since developer support pages will usually give more information than the App Store. And to squeeze more out of what's already on your wrist, there are plenty of underrated Apple Watch features you can set up in minutes.

#328. Protesters Throw Projectiles at Biden During Dublin Trip

Video showed demonstrators from a pro-Palestinian protest throwing projectiles at former President Joseph R. Biden Jr. after he attended an event at Trinity College Dublin on Tuesday.

Protesters threw projectiles at former President Joseph R. Biden Jr. after he attended an event at Trinity College Dublin on Tuesday, as the police scuffled with demonstrators attending a pro-Palestinian rally, according to video of the incident.

An Garda Síochána, the Irish national police force, said three men had been arrested on Tuesday in relation to a public order incident. Two of the men were later released, and one was charged, the police said in a statement on Wednesday.

Video of the episode showed Mr. Biden being shielded from the projectiles by black umbrellas held by members of his entourage.

Mr. Biden had been attending a ceremony honoring his son, Hunter Biden, by a debating society that praised him for speaking publicly about politics and his struggle with addiction. Hunter Biden and Jill Biden, the former first lady, also attended the event, according to Ireland’s national broadcaster, RTÉ.

“A protest took place in Trinity College Dublin’s Front Square on Tuesday, 10 November during a ceremony in the Exam Hall,” said Catherine O’Mahony, a spokeswoman for the college. “The protest escalated while the Bidens were leaving” the event, she said.

Videos show groups of people gathered in the square, some waving Palestinian flags and chanting “blood on your hands.” As Mr. Biden was leaving the area, footage shows objects and white liquid, which appears to be milk, being thrown at him.

#326. Rocket Report: Starship set for historic test flight; a century of Electron

“You can simplify it as a big tank feeding engines.”

Welcome to Edition 9.19 of the Rocket Report! Will something historic happen this weekend? No orbital rocket has ever been fully recovered with the intent of reusing all of its components. But that’s just what SpaceX is going to try to do with a Starship launch on Friday, and an upper stage landing attempt 22.5 hours later on Saturday afternoon, local time. Ars will be on hand in Starbase, Texas, to provide coverage of it all.

Electron set for milestone launch. The next launch of Rocket Lab’s Electron vehicle is due to lift off from the Mahia Peninsula in New Zealand on November 14 at 5:30 UTC. This mission will serve as Electron’s 100th overall mission—a notable milestone for the small rocket that first flew in 2017, NASASpaceflight.com reports.

A true commercial success … This flight of Electron, named “The Mountain God Rises,” will deliver another iQPS satellite into LEO for iQPS’s synthetic aperture radar constellation. The anniversary rocket features a special gold-and-black livery which looks fantastic. Rocket Lab truly does deserve recognition as the world’s second purely commercial launch business to make a successful go at it. We are all celebrating with them.

Is the Vega rocket a dead end? Last month, Italian rocket builder Avio presented a market update that outlined the additional investment required to increase the annual launch cadence of its Vega C rocket to six and eventually nine flights per year, European Spaceflight reports. The need for this additional funding raises an interesting question about the future of Italy’s Vega launch vehicle family. Is investing in the infrastructure needed to secure just three more Vega C flights per year by the end of the decade the best use of resources, particularly when several emerging European launch companies appear poised to offer comparable capacity?

Boosters may be better used by Ariane 6 … Vega C isn’t going anywhere. But it’s an inescapable reality that a single Ariane 64 launch requires the equivalent of an entire year’s worth of solid rocket boosters for Vega C at its baseline annual launch cadence of four flights. Does it make sense to continue investing in expanding Vega C’s launch cadence and later introducing Vega E when the future of both vehicles depends on production capacity that is increasingly demanded by Ariane 6?

Synspective inks 10 Alpha rockets. Firefly Aerospace announced on Tuesday a multi-launch agreement with Synspective, a Japanese synthetic aperture radar satellite data and solutions provider, for up to 10 launches on Firefly’s Alpha rocket through 2030. With the ability to launch 1,000 kg to low Earth orbit, Alpha will deliver two of Synspective’s SAR satellites to orbit per mission, deploying up to 20 total satellites.

Getting it done with one ton … Under the agreement, Firefly will launch Synspective’s SAR satellites from both Pad-0A at Wallops Flight Facility in Virginia and Space Launch Complex 2 at Vandenberg Space Force Base in California. “This landmark agreement reflects growing customer confidence in our Alpha Block II vehicle,” said Jason Kim, CEO of Firefly Aerospace. “With 1-ton payload capacity and responsive launch capabilities, Alpha is a natural fit for customers like Synspective seeking direct access to orbit to get their operations up and running sooner.”

Stoke and Planet sign multi-launch agreement. Stoke Space on Monday announced a multi-launch agreement with Planet Labs PBC. The companies did not announce the terms of the agreement, including the total number of launches under contract, nor the cost of the launches. “We need launch partners who move as quickly as we do,” said Will Marshall, Co-Founder & CEO of Planet.

An open-ended agreement? … The announcement suggests this could be an open-ended agreement, however. “Planet builds and operates the largest fleet of Earth-imaging satellites in orbit and captures imagery of Earth’s landmass every day,” a related release says. “Operators like Planet launch on a regular basis to expand and replenish their fleets, and that steady demand is what our Nova fleet is designed to serve.”

The launch crunch comes to national security. The US military is taking a new approach to prop up commercial launch companies as SpaceX looks to wind down its Falcon rocket program, suggesting defense officials see the workhorse rocket’s retirement as a potential national security risk, Ars reports. The Pentagon’s Office of Strategic Capital has twice in the last two weeks announced it was sending cash to two of SpaceX’s competitors in the launch business.

More pads and rockets … First, on October 26, the office announced a $150 million conditional loan commitment to Stoke Space. Military officials revealed a second $150 million Pentagon loan Tuesday for Rocket Lab. Stoke Space’s loan is tailored to support the buildout of the company’s second launch pad at Cape Canaveral Space Force Station, Florida. The loan to Rocket Lab will support the company’s efforts to increase the flight rate of its partially reusable Neutron rocket.

Rocket Lab raises Neutron price. Citing strong customer demand and a constrained market for launch, Rocket Lab announced this week it had increased the cost of a dedicated Neutron rocket from $55 million to $70 million, Payload reports. In recent months, the coming shortage of launch capacity in the US—mainly due to SpaceX sunsetting its Transporter rideshare program—has sparked a flurry of interest in new medium-lift rocket entrants.

Positive on Neutron … “Neutron is rapidly establishing itself as the backbone of next-generation constellation deployment and government missions in the medium-lift launch class,” CEO Peter Beck said in a statement. “Strong international demand and a growing launch manifest, at a new price point, is proof that Neutron is the launch vehicle the market has been waiting for.” The price hike for Neutron isn’t keeping customers away as new bookings continue, the company said. Customers’ next options to fly on Neutron are now in the 2030s and beyond.

Rockets are not hard? During an hour-long event on Thursday, Abel Avellan, the founder and chief executive of the telecommunications company AST SpaceMobile, laid out his vision for developing a large rocket to launch his Bluebird satellites into orbit, Ars reports. Avellan emphasized, over and over again, that AST plans to build a “simple” rocket. He paraphrased SpaceX founder Elon Musk several times, saying, “the best part is no part.”

This sounds a little naive … “Of course rocket engineers are going to get mad with me, but you can simplify it as a big tank feeding engines,” he said of the rocket. “So big tanks—we know how to do them. We know how to do them. We know how to do them in composite.” The Blacklift rocket will be “simple,” he said, because it will be solely tailored to lift five Bluebird satellites into low-Earth orbit at a time. It will have 20 metric tons of lift capacity, a reusable first stage, and launch twice a month from a pad at Wallops Flight Facility in Virginia that formerly served the Antares rocket. (submitted by thegooglemonster)

When will the Eclipse rocket be ready? During an earnings call this week (see transcript), Firefly CEO Kim spoke about the company’s ongoing work to develop the Eclipse rocket. “We’re heads down on Eclipse,” he said. “We’re laser-focused on delivering the first stage to our co-developer Northrop Grumman. And we’re over 175 hot fires on Miranda, counting the one from today. And we’re looking at all the data, verifying the capability. It’s a very mature engine, and we’re very confident in its capabilities.”

Probably not launching soon … However, when an analyst pressed on Firefly getting a launch in 2027, Kim did not offer a direct answer. “Everything is just laser-focused on all the milestones in terms of qualifying Miranda and qualifying our composite tanks and fluid systems as well,” he said. “So we’re really, really just excited about the future of Eclipse, especially with this injection of capital that will help accelerate our production line.” Bottom line: Don’t expect to see Eclipse on a launch pad any time soon.

Starship set for 15th test flight on Friday. Flight 15 of Starship is preparing to launch as soon as Friday, November 13, pending regulatory approval, SpaceX said. The 75-minute launch window will open at 4:45 p.m. CT (22:45 UTC). The upcoming flight is planned to be the first to return both Starship and Super Heavy to the launch site for catch. If successful, this will mark the first full recovery of an orbital launch system.

All eyes on the ship … Starship’s initial return-to-launch-site mission is expected to orbit the Earth at an altitude of about 275 km and complete approximately 14 orbits around the planet over the course of a more than 22-hour flight. Starship’s primary mission will be to deliver 26 Starlink V3 satellites to orbit. But really, this mission is all about the landings, first of the booster and then, more dramatically, of the upper stage Starship on Saturday.

SpaceX is now an ‘infrastructure’ company. For a long time, SpaceX has been synonymous with developing newer, larger, and ever-more-reusable rockets, Ars reports. But that began to change over the last decade with the introduction of Starlink, and the change has accelerated during the last 18 months as the company has pivoted to data and artificial intelligence. At last week’s UP.Summit conference in Florida, SpaceX’s vice president of launch, Kiko Dontchev, offered some of the most revealing comments to date about the company’s changing focus.

From AI to Mars? … “In the last couple years, when I talk about SpaceX, yes, we are a rocket company, but fundamentally we are an infrastructure company at this point,” Dontchev said. “We’re building infrastructure on the ground and low Earth orbit, soon on the Moon, and obviously eventually Mars.” However, Dontchev insisted that human settlement and Mars remain part of the core of SpaceX’s aspirations. “We have come to understand that this tool is critical to us accelerating our pace of innovation,” he said of artificial intelligence. “Without AI, I think we still would have gotten to the Moon. I think we still get to Mars with SI. We’re going to get there so much faster.”

Nov. 13: Vulcan | Amazon Leo LV-01 | Cape Canaveral Space Force Station, Florida | 17:54 UTC

Nov. 13: Starship | Flight 15 | Starbase, Texas | 22:45 UTC
